No structs, enums, typedefs, classes, or other user-defined types are defined in this header. It only declares integer-like error code macros via #define. The closest related type is the builtin int that these macros expand to in expressions, but there is no typedef alias defined here.

objects.definition: using LogCallback    = std::function<void(int, const char*, const char*)>;
objects.description: Alias for a logging callback taking level/code and two C-string messages. Intended to be invoked with three parameters: an int and two const char* values. It is a std::function wrapper type.

objects.definition: using NotifyCallback = std::function<void(int, int, int, void*, int)>;
objects.description: Alias for a notification callback accepting five parameters: three ints, a generic pointer payload, and an int (likely size or tag). It is a std::function wrapper type.
Alias for an injection or IO callback that takes a context pointer, an int (e.g., command or size), and a data pointer, returning an int status/result. It is a std::function wrapper type.

Holds codec and stream parameters for a single media track. Includes common fields, video-specific settings (dimensions, SAR, FPS, time base, pixel/color info), and audio-specific settings (channels, sample format/rate). May own an extra_data buffer (codec extradata) that should be heap-allocated and later freed. Lifetime is managed by owners; no custom destructor here.

Container for media-level metadata, including duration, bitrate, start time, and selected stream indices. Owns a vector of TrackInfo entries and, via the destructor, assumes ownership of each entry’s extra_data, freeing it with delete[].

Enumeration of control requests that can be issued to a player: start, pause, seek, kernel-level pause, and play speed change. Values are large distinct integer codes suitable for IPC or message passing. No additional semantics or construction details are provided in this header.

Enumeration of value kinds that entries in NextDictionary can store. Used to discriminate the stored payload in an Item. Note: VALUE_TYPE_INT32 is defined but no int32 storage is currently present in Item; likely reserved for future use.

A heterogenous key/value dictionary supporting string keys and values of types indicated by ValueType. Public API allows storing and retrieving int64 and std::string values, querying size, and enumerating entry names with types. Internally owns a vector of Item* representing entries. Destructor and Clear are responsible for releasing Item allocations and associated value memory. Construction is default; copy/move semantics are not declared (compiler defaults apply if definition allows).

Holds log configuration/state for the logging system: a minimum log level threshold, an opaque userdata pointer, and a callback receiving log messages. The callback is invoked with the provided userdata, the message level, and a C-string buffer for the formatted message. Lifetime and allocation of LogContext are not defined in this header; it is a plain aggregate intended to be stack- or heap-allocated by the user.

Utility class providing static inline helpers to parse H.264/AVC and HEVC/H.265 NAL unit headers from a bytestream-like buffer. It extracts NAL unit type, reference idc, HEVC layer id, and classifies IDR and non-reference VCL types. No instances are needed; all methods are static. Depends on constants/macros like NAL_IDR_SLICE and HEVC_NAL_* presumed to be defined in NextDefine.h. Note: get_hevc_nuh_layer_id likely intends to parse nuh_layer_id from bytes 4-5 of the NAL header; operator precedence may need parentheses to ensure correct bit extraction.

functions.name: ByteToInt
functions.description: Converts a 4-byte big-endian sequence starting at src into a 32-bit unsigned integer. Useful for parsing network-order or file-format fields stored in big-endian byte arrays.
requirements: src must be a valid, non-null pointer to at least 4 readable bytes.
The 4 bytes at src are interpreted as big-endian order (src[0] is the most significant byte).
Function is pure and thread-safe; it has no side effects.
Behavior is undefined if src is null or does not point to at least 4 bytes.

functions.name: CurrentTimeUs
functions.description: Returns the current wall-clock time since the Unix epoch in microseconds using std::chrono::system_clock. Intended for timestamping or measuring wall-clock intervals with microsecond granularity, subject to system clock resolution.
requirements: No arguments required; callable at any time.
Return value represents system_clock time since epoch; it may jump forwards or backwards if the system clock is adjusted (not monotonic).
Precision and accuracy depend on the platform’s system_clock resolution.

functions.name: CurrentTimeMs
functions.description: Returns the current wall-clock time since the Unix epoch in milliseconds using std::chrono::system_clock. Intended for timestamping or coarse interval measurement with millisecond granularity, subject to system clock resolution.
requirements: No arguments required; callable at any time.
Return value represents system_clock time since epoch; it may jump forwards or backwards if the system clock is adjusted (not monotonic).
Precision and accuracy depend on the platform’s system_clock resolution.

functions.name: NextDictionary::~NextDictionary
functions.description: Destroys a NextDictionary instance and releases any resources owned by it (such as stored items and their values). Intended to be called automatically when an instance goes out of scope or is deleted through a pointer to NextDictionary.
requirements: Object must not be used after destruction.
If deleted through a base-class pointer, the destructor is virtual to ensure proper cleanup.

functions.name: NextDictionary::Clear
functions.description: Removes all entries from the dictionary and resets it to an empty state. Use to reuse an instance without destroying it.
requirements: The NextDictionary instance must be valid/initialized when called.
All iterators or indices previously obtained (e.g., via GetEntryNameAt) become invalid after this call.

functions.name: NextDictionary::SetInt64
functions.description: Associates the key given by name with a 64-bit integer value, inserting or replacing the entry for that key.
requirements: name must be a valid, null-terminated C string pointer (non-null).

Behavior regarding whether the key string is copied or referenced is unknown from the header; callers should not assume anything about the lifetime requirements of name based solely on this declaration.

functions.name: NextDictionary::FindInt64
functions.description: Looks up the 64-bit integer value associated with name. Returns true if found and, on success, writes the value to the output pointer.
requirements: name must be a valid, null-terminated C string pointer (non-null).
value should be a valid, non-null pointer if the caller expects the found value to be written.
If the key is not found, the function returns false and the content of *value is unspecified.

functions.name: NextDictionary::GetInt64
functions.signature: int64_t NextDictionary::GetInt64(const char *name, int64_t defaultValue) const;
functions.description: Retrieves the 64-bit integer value for name, or returns defaultValue if the key does not exist.
requirements: name must be a valid, null-terminated C string pointer (non-null).

functions.name: NextDictionary::SetString
functions.description: Associates the key given by name with a string value, inserting or replacing the entry for that key.
requirements: name must be a valid, null-terminated C string pointer (non-null).

Behavior regarding whether the key string is copied or referenced is unknown from the header; callers should not assume anything about the lifetime requirements of name based solely on this declaration.

functions.name: NextDictionary::GetString
functions.description: Retrieves the string value for name. If the key does not exist, the returned value may be derived from defaultValue (exact semantics are not specified in the header).
requirements: name must be a valid, null-terminated C string pointer (non-null).
defaultValue may be used as a fallback when the key is missing; precise behavior when defaultValue is null is unknown from the header.

functions.name: NextDictionary::GetSize
functions.description: Returns the number of entries currently stored in the dictionary.

functions.name: NextDictionary::GetEntryNameAt
functions.description: Returns the key name for the entry at the given zero-based index and optionally writes the entry’s value type to type. Intended for iterating entries by index.
requirements: index must be in the range [0, GetSize()).
type should be a valid pointer if the caller wants the value type to be written; passing null to ignore the type is a common pattern but not explicitly stated.
The returned const char* remains valid at least until the dictionary is modified; exact lifetime guarantees are not specified in the header.

functions.name: LogPrint
functions.signature: int LogPrint(int level, const char *tag, const char *fmt, ...);
functions.description: Formats and emits a log message at the given severity level with a textual tag. Variadic arguments follow printf-style formatting specified by fmt. Output handling may be influenced by SetLogLevel (to filter by severity) and SetLogCallback (to redirect messages to a user callback). The precise return value and default output destination are not documented in this header and are unknown.
requirements: level must be a valid logging level as defined by AV_LEVEL_FATAL, AV_LEVEL_ERROR, AV_LEVEL_WARN, AV_LEVEL_INFO, or AV_LEVEL_DEBUG.
tag must be a valid, null-terminated C string pointer.
fmt must be a valid, null-terminated printf-style format string.
The variadic arguments must match the format specifiers in fmt (printf-style semantics).
If using a custom callback via SetLogCallback, the callback and userdata must have been previously set and remain valid at the time of the call.

functions.name: SetLogLevel
functions.description: Sets the global logging threshold/level used to filter which messages are emitted. Subsequent LogPrint (or macros that call it) will be subject to this level. Exact filtering semantics are not documented here; it is expected that the level corresponds to the AV_LEVEL_* constants.
requirements: level must be a valid logging level as defined by AV_LEVEL_FATAL, AV_LEVEL_ERROR, AV_LEVEL_WARN, AV_LEVEL_INFO, or AV_LEVEL_DEBUG.

functions.name: SetLogCallback
functions.signature: void SetLogCallback(void (*callback)(void *, int, const char *), void *userdata);
functions.description: Registers a user-provided logging callback that, when set, will receive log messages. The callback is invoked with the provided userdata, the message level, and a C string buffer containing the formatted message. Whether passing NULL clears the callback is not specified in this header and is unknown.
requirements: callback must point to a function with signature void(void *userdata, int level, const char *buf).
userdata is an opaque pointer provided by the caller; it must remain valid for as long as the callback may be invoked or until SetLogCallback is called again to change it.
The callback must be able to safely read buf as a null-terminated C string for the duration of the call.
level passed to the callback will correspond to the AV_LEVEL_* constants.

functions.name: NEXT_LOGD
functions.description: Convenience, function-like variadic macro for emitting a debug-level log message. It expands to LogPrint(AV_LEVEL_DEBUG, tag, fmt, ...). Use it to record detailed diagnostic information that may be filtered by the current log level. Returns whatever LogPrint returns.
requirements: This is a macro that forwards to: int LogPrint(int level, const char *tag, const char *fmt, ...).
Must be invoked with at least two arguments: tag and fmt, followed by optional format arguments.
tag should point to a null-terminated C string identifying the log source; behavior for NULL is unspecified.
fmt should be a valid printf-style format string, null-terminated.
If fmt contains format specifiers, the provided variadic arguments must match in count and compatible types (printf-style).
The macro sets level to AV_LEVEL_DEBUG automatically; callers must not supply level.

functions.name: NEXT_LOGI
functions.description: Convenience, function-like variadic macro for emitting an info-level log message. It expands to LogPrint(AV_LEVEL_INFO, tag, fmt, ...). Use it for general informational messages. Returns whatever LogPrint returns.
requirements: This is a macro that forwards to: int LogPrint(int level, const char *tag, const char *fmt, ...).
Must be invoked with at least two arguments: tag and fmt, followed by optional format arguments.
tag should point to a null-terminated C string identifying the log source; behavior for NULL is unspecified.
fmt should be a valid printf-style format string, null-terminated.
If fmt contains format specifiers, the provided variadic arguments must match in count and compatible types (printf-style).
The macro sets level to AV_LEVEL_INFO automatically; callers must not supply level.

requirements: This is a macro that forwards to: int LogPrint(int level, const char *tag, const char *fmt, ...).
Must be invoked with at least two arguments: tag and fmt, followed by optional format arguments.
tag should point to a null-terminated C string identifying the log source; behavior for NULL is unspecified.
fmt should be a valid printf-style format string, null-terminated.

functions.name: NEXT_LOGE
functions.description: Convenience, function-like variadic macro for emitting an error-level log message. It expands to LogPrint(AV_LEVEL_ERROR, tag, fmt, ...). Use it to report errors or failures. Returns whatever LogPrint returns.
requirements: This is a macro that forwards to: int LogPrint(int level, const char *tag, const char *fmt, ...).
Must be invoked with at least two arguments: tag and fmt, followed by optional format arguments.
tag should point to a null-terminated C string identifying the log source; behavior for NULL is unspecified.
fmt should be a valid printf-style format string, null-terminated.
If fmt contains format specifiers, the provided variadic arguments must match in count and compatible types (printf-style).

functions.name: NALUnitParser::get_h264_nal_unit_type
functions.description: Returns the H.264 NAL unit type parsed from the header byte assumed to be at data[4]. Intended for Annex B formatted access units where a 4-byte start code precedes the NAL header. Usage: pass a pointer to a buffer positioned at the start of a NAL unit that begins with a 4-byte start code; this function extracts the 5-bit type field (bits 0–4) from the first byte of the NAL header.
requirements: data must be non-null.
data must reference at least 5 bytes (index 0..4) because this function reads data[4].

The buffer layout is assumed to be Annex B with a 4-byte start code (0x00000001) before the NAL header; data[4] is the NAL header byte. If the header is elsewhere (e.g., length-prefixed format), adjust the pointer accordingly.
The returned type is the raw 5-bit H.264 NAL unit type; callers should ensure the input actually corresponds to H.264.

functions.name: NALUnitParser::get_hevc_nal_unit_type
functions.description: Returns the HEVC (H.265) NAL unit type parsed from the header byte assumed to be at data[4]. It extracts bits 1–6 of the first HEVC header byte: (data[4] & 0x7E) >> 1. Usage: pass a buffer positioned at an HEVC NAL unit with a preceding 4-byte start code.
requirements: data must be non-null.
data must reference at least 5 bytes (index 0..4).
The buffer is assumed Annex B with a 4-byte start code; data[4] is the first NAL header byte. If using length-prefixed streams, point data to the header byte instead.
The returned value is the 6-bit HEVC NAL unit type; callers should ensure the input is HEVC.

functions.name: NALUnitParser::is_h264_idr
functions.description: Returns nonzero if the provided H.264 NAL unit type corresponds to an IDR slice. It compares the type against NAL_IDR_SLICE (from NextDefine.h). Usage: obtain a type via get_h264_nal_unit_type and pass it here.
requirements: type must be a valid H.264 NAL unit type value as defined by the H.264 spec and constants in NextDefine.h.
NextDefine.h must define NAL_IDR_SLICE; otherwise this cannot be evaluated.

functions.name: NALUnitParser::is_hevc_idr
functions.description: Returns nonzero if the provided HEVC NAL unit type is an IDR/BLA/CRA access point type. It checks against HEVC_NAL_BLA_W_LP, HEVC_NAL_BLA_W_RADL, HEVC_NAL_BLA_N_LP, HEVC_NAL_IDR_W_RADL, HEVC_NAL_IDR_N_LP, and HEVC_NAL_CRA_NUT (constants expected in NextDefine.h). Usage: obtain a type via get_hevc_nal_unit_type and pass it here.
requirements: type must be a valid HEVC NAL unit type per the HEVC spec.
NextDefine.h must define the HEVC_NAL_* constants used; otherwise this cannot be evaluated.

functions.name: NALUnitParser::is_hevc_no_ref
functions.description: Returns true if the provided HEVC NAL unit type is a non-reference VCL picture (TRAIL_N, TSA_N, STSA_N, RADL_N, RASL_N, VCL_N10, VCL_N12, VCL_N14). Usage: obtain a type via get_hevc_nal_unit_type and pass it here to identify non-reference frames.
requirements: type must be a valid HEVC NAL unit type value.
NextDefine.h must define the HEVC_NAL_* constants used (HEVC_NAL_TRAIL_N, HEVC_NAL_TSA_N, HEVC_NAL_STSA_N, HEVC_NAL_RADL_N, HEVC_NAL_RASL_N, HEVC_NAL_VCL_N10, HEVC_NAL_VCL_N12, HEVC_NAL_VCL_N14).

functions.name: NALUnitParser::get_h264_ref_idc
functions.description: Extracts the H.264 nal_ref_idc from the NAL header byte assumed to be at data[4]. It returns the 2-bit reference IDC ((data[4] >> 5) & 0x03), indicating the reference importance of the NAL unit. Usage: pass a buffer positioned at an H.264 NAL header following a 4-byte start code.
requirements: data must be non-null.
data must reference at least 5 bytes (index 0..4).
The buffer is assumed Annex B with a 4-byte start code; data[4] is the NAL header byte.
Only valid for H.264 NAL headers; callers must ensure the buffer is H.264.

functions.name: NALUnitParser::get_hevc_nuh_layer_id
functions.description: Returns the HEVC nuh_layer_id computed from data[4] and data[5] as implemented: (data[4] & 0x1 << 5) + (data[5] >> 3) & 0x1F. Intended to extract the 6-bit nuh_layer_id field spanning the last bit of the first header byte and the high 5 bits of the second header byte. Note: The current implementation effectively computes (data[4] & 0x20) + ((data[5] >> 3) & 0x1F). This differs from the typical formula ((data[4] & 0x01) << 5) | ((data[5] >> 3) & 0x1F); use with caution or verify against the spec.
requirements: data must be non-null.
data must reference at least 6 bytes (index 0..5).
Assumes Annex B with a 4-byte start code; data[4] and data[5] are the first two bytes of the HEVC NAL header.
Callers should verify the stream is HEVC; otherwise the result is meaningless.
Be aware that the bit extraction as written may not match the HEVC spec; validate for your use case.

data_types.description: Arbitrary uninterpreted bytes. May contain any 8-bit values and be of variable length. Used when a function reads raw bytes without assuming text encoding or specific structure beyond byte positions.
A null-terminated text string passed via std::string::c_str(). Expected to be valid UTF-8 or generic ASCII text. No specific content restrictions beyond being a text key or tag.
A C-style format string for printf-like functions. Contains percent-format specifiers matching provided variadic arguments (e.g., %d, %s, %x). Must be null-terminated.

Raw byte buffer representing an Annex B formatted NAL unit region with a 4-byte start code 0x00000001 followed by codec header bytes at specific offsets. The stubs enforce indices 0..3 as the start code and place header bytes at offsets 4 (and 5). Used for parsing H.264 or HEVC NAL header fields.

import random
from typing import List

# We need to generate a variable-size binary blob that is likely valid for the ByteToInt fuzzer stub.
# The stub requires at least 4 bytes, and it may choose any offset within the blob such that 4 bytes are readable.
# To exercise interesting behaviors, we produce buffers containing multiple 4-byte big-endian segments with
# recognizable patterns (zeros, ones, max values, alternating patterns, random values, aligned and misaligned positions),
# and variable overall sizes. This increases chances that the chosen random offset hits an interesting 4-byte pattern.

MAX_SIZE = 4096


def _be32(x: int) -> bytes:
    x &= 0xFFFFFFFF
    return bytes([(x >> 24) & 0xFF, (x >> 16) & 0xFF, (x >> 8) & 0xFF, x & 0xFF])


def _append_pattern(buf: bytearray, chunks: List[bytes], repeat: int = 1) -> None:
    for _ in range(repeat):
        for c in chunks:
            buf.extend(c)


def _interesting_be32_values(rng: random.Random) -> List[int]:
    # Include edge cases and a few randoms
    vals = [
        0x00000000,
        0x00000001,
        0x0000007F,
        0x00000080,
        0x000000FF,
        0x00007FFF,
        0x00008000,
        0x0000FFFF,
        0x7FFFFFFF,
        0x80000000,
        0xFFFFFFFF,
        0x01020304,
        0x11223344,
        0xA5A5A5A5,
        0x5A5A5A5A,
        0xDEADBEEF,
        0xFEEDFACE,
        0xCAFEBABE,
    ]
    # Add several random 32-bit values
    for _ in range(8):
        vals.append(rng.getrandbits(32))
    return vals


def _pad_with_noise(buf: bytearray, rng: random.Random, target_size: int) -> None:
    # Fill remaining space with random noise to create many possible offsets.
    remaining = max(0, target_size - len(buf))
    if remaining <= 0:
        return
    # Mix of structured small patterns and random bytes
    patterns = [
        b"\x00\x00\x00\x00",
        b"\xFF\xFF\xFF\xFF",
        b"\xAA\xAA\xAA\xAA",
        b"\x55\x55\x55\x55",
        b"\x00\x00\x00\x01",
        b"\x01\x00\x00\x00",
    ]
    i = 0
    while i < remaining:
        choice = rng.randrange(3)
        if choice == 0 and patterns:
            p = rng.choice(patterns)
            take = min(len(p), remaining - i)
            buf.extend(p[:take])
            i += take
        elif choice == 1:
            # random aligned 4-byte chunk
            val = rng.getrandbits(32)
            b = _be32(val)
            take = min(4, remaining - i)
            buf.extend(b[:take])
            i += take
        else:
            # single random byte
            buf.append(rng.randrange(256))
            i += 1


def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rng = random.Random(seed)

    # Decide total size in [4, 1024] with bias to larger buffers but cap at MAX_SIZE
    # Larger buffers give more offsets; still bounded for performance.
    sizes = [4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 768, 1024]
    total_size = min(MAX_SIZE, rng.choice(sizes))

    buf = bytearray()

    # Ensure at least one 4-byte chunk at start for offset=0
    vals = _interesting_be32_values(rng)
    rng.shuffle(vals)

    # Build a header region with several interesting big-endian 32-bit ints, including start code-like sequences
    header_chunks = []
    # Annex B start codes for potential NAL header parsing (though ByteToInt doesn't require it, useful for broader reuse)
    header_chunks.append(b"\x00\x00\x00\x01")  # 4-byte start code
    header_chunks.append(b"\x00\x00\x01\xE0")  # 3-byte + next byte
    header_chunks.append(_be32(vals[0]))
    header_chunks.append(_be32(vals[1]))
    header_chunks.append(b"\x12\x34\x56\x78")
    header_chunks.append(b"\x87\x65\x43\x21")

    _append_pattern(buf, header_chunks)

    # Insert misaligned 4-byte sequences by adding 1–3 prefix noise bytes before some sequences
    for v in vals[2:8]:
        mis = rng.randrange(1, 4)
        buf.extend(bytes([rng.randrange(256) for _ in range(mis)]))
        buf.extend(_be32(v))
        if len(buf) >= total_size:
            break

    # Add a block of repeating patterns to exercise repeated values
    repeat_block = [_be32(0xFFFFFFFF), _be32(0x00000000), _be32(0x7FFFFFFF), _be32(0x80000000)]
    _append_pattern(buf, repeat_block, repeat=2)

    # Ensure at least 4 bytes even if size was tiny
    if len(buf) < 4:
        buf.extend(b"\x00" * (4 - len(buf)))

    # Pad/truncate to target size
    if len(buf) < total_size:
        _pad_with_noise(buf, rng, total_size)
    elif len(buf) > total_size:
        del buf[total_size:]

    # Guarantee last 4 bytes form an interesting big-endian value so offsets near end are valid and meaningful
    if total_size >= 4:
        tail_val = rng.choice(_interesting_be32_values(rng))
        tail = _be32(tail_val)
        buf[-4:] = tail

    return bytes(buf)

import random
import struct
import string
from typing import List

# This generator targets fuzzers that consume ASCII/UTF-8 strings via FUZZ_PARAM_STR
# and integers via FUZZ_PARAM(int64_t)/unsigned int. We build a single bytes blob
# that the harness slices to provide these parameters. We therefore pack a small
# corpus of interesting strings followed by integers. All strings are null-terminated.
# Keep total size <= 4096 bytes.

# Layout:
# [u32 num_strings]
#   repeated num_strings times: [u32 len][bytes str(len)][\0]
# [u32 num_int64]
#   repeated num_int64: [int64]
# [u32 num_uint]
#   repeated num_uint: [u32]
# [padding optional]
#
# This allows the fuzzer runtime to draw from a pool of key/tag/default strings and
# integer values, exercising SetInt64/FindInt64/GetInt64/SetString/GetString and
# logging APIs with valid data.

MAX_TOTAL = 4096

# Interesting edge-case strings for keys/tags/defaults
BASE_STRINGS = [
    "",  # empty key/tag
    "a",
    "0",
    "key",
    "value",
    "debug",
    "info",
    "warn",
    "error",
    "id",
    "name",
    "hex",
    "视频",  # non-ASCII UTF-8
    "ключ",  # Cyrillic
    "emoji_😀",
    "long_key_" + ("x" * 128),
    "path/with/slash",
    "key.with.dots",
    "UPPER_lower_Mixed",
    "spaces in key",
]

# Pairs that encourage collisions and overwrites in the dictionary
MUTUAL_KEYS = [
    ("k", "k"),
    ("key", "key"),
    ("Key", "key"),
    ("ä", "a"),  # utf-8 vs ascii similar
]

# Interesting int64 values
BASE_I64 = [
    0,
    1,
    -1,
    2**63 - 1,
    -2**63,
    2**31 - 1,
    -2**31,
    10,
    60,
    1000,
    1000000,
]

# Interesting unsigned ints for log levels, selectors, etc.
BASE_U32 = [
    0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5,
    0xFFFFFFFF,
    7, 9, 10, 16, 31, 63, 127, 255,
]


def _rand_utf8(rng: random.Random, min_len: int = 0, max_len: int = 40) -> str:
    # Mix ASCII and selected Unicode ranges
    length = rng.randint(min_len, max_len)
    choices: List[str] = []
    # ASCII letters/digits/punct
    choices += list(string.ascii_letters + string.digits + " _-./:")
    # A few ranges of BMP unicode characters
    def add_range(start, end):
        for cp in range(start, end + 1):
            try:
                ch = chr(cp)
                ch.encode('utf-8')
                choices.append(ch)
            except Exception:
                pass
    # Add a small subset to avoid huge choice list
    for start, end, step in [(0x0400, 0x042F, 1), (0x4E00, 0x4E2F, 1), (0x03B1, 0x03C1, 1)]:
        for cp in range(start, end + 1):
            try:
                ch = chr(cp)
                ch.encode('utf-8')
                choices.append(ch)
            except Exception:
                continue
    if not choices:
        choices = list(string.ascii_letters)
    s = ''.join(rng.choice(choices) for _ in range(length))
    return s


def _build_strings(rng: random.Random) -> List[str]:
    strings: List[str] = []
    # Seed with base set
    strings.extend(BASE_STRINGS)

    # Add paired duplicates/near-duplicates
    for a, b in MUTUAL_KEYS:
        strings.append(a)
        strings.append(b)

    # Randomly synthesize more keys/values/tags
    extra = rng.randint(8, 20)
    for _ in range(extra):
        s = _rand_utf8(rng, 0, rng.randint(5, 60))
        strings.append(s)

    # Ensure format-like tokens to drive branches
    strings += [
        "plain message",
        "value=%d",
        "id=%d name=%s hex=%x",
        "cb test %d %s",
        "debug plain",
        "dbg=%d",
        "d:%d %s %x",
        "info plain",
        "info=%d",
        "i:%d %s %x",
        "warn plain",
        "warn=%d",
        "w:%d %s %x",
        "error plain",
        "err=%d",
        "e:%d %s %x",
        "fuzz",
    ]

    # De-duplicate while preserving order
    seen = set()
    uniq: List[str] = []
    for s in strings:
        if s not in seen:
            seen.add(s)
            uniq.append(s)
    return uniq


def _build_ints(rng: random.Random) -> List[int]:
    vals = list(BASE_I64)
    # Some random bounded values
    for _ in range(rng.randint(10, 20)):
        vals.append(rng.randint(-2**63, 2**63 - 1))
    # Bias towards small domain for log levels/selectors
    vals += [rng.randint(0, 7) for _ in range(8)]
    # Potential dictionary-related sizes
    vals += [3, 16, 9, 256, 1024, 4096]
    # Make unique while preserving order
    seen = set()
    out: List[int] = []
    for v in vals:
        if v not in seen:
            seen.add(v)
            out.append(v)
    return out


def _build_uints(rng: random.Random) -> List[int]:
    vals = list(BASE_U32)
    # Some random values, including masked ranges for selectors
    for _ in range(rng.randint(10, 20)):
        v = rng.getrandbits(32)
        vals.append(v)
        vals.append(v % 3)
        vals.append(v % 5)
    # Unique preserve order
    seen = set()
    out: List[int] = []
    for v in vals:
        if v not in seen:
            seen.add(v)
            out.append(v)
    return out


def _pack_strings(buf: bytearray, strings: List[str]):
    buf.extend(struct.pack('>I', len(strings)))
    for s in strings:
        b = s.encode('utf-8', errors='strict')
        # ensure one NUL terminator for c_str() use
        buf.extend(struct.pack('>I', len(b)))
        buf.extend(b)
        buf.append(0)


def _pack_i64(buf: bytearray, ints: List[int]):
    buf.extend(struct.pack('>I', len(ints)))
    for v in ints:
        buf.extend(struct.pack('>q', int(v)))


def _pack_u32(buf: bytearray, uints: List[int]):
    buf.extend(struct.pack('>I', len(uints)))
    for v in uints:
        buf.extend(struct.pack('>I', int(v) & 0xFFFFFFFF))


def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rng = random.Random(seed)

    strings = _build_strings(rng)
    ints = _build_ints(rng)
    uints = _build_uints(rng)

    # Assemble buffer
    buf = bytearray()
    _pack_strings(buf, strings)
    _pack_i64(buf, ints)
    _pack_u32(buf, uints)

    # Trim if exceeding max, but keep header integrity by truncating strings/arrays gracefully.
    if len(buf) > MAX_TOTAL:
        # Simple strategy: reduce strings payload until within limit
        # Rebuild with fewer strings
        keep = max(8, int(len(strings) * 0.6))
        strings = strings[:keep]
        buf = bytearray()
        _pack_strings(buf, strings)
        _pack_i64(buf, ints)
        _pack_u32(buf, uints)
        if len(buf) > MAX_TOTAL:
            # As a last resort, drop some random tails
            # Recompute target sizes proportionally
            scale = MAX_TOTAL / max(1, len(buf))
            k_ints = max(8, int(len(ints) * scale))
            k_uints = max(8, int(len(uints) * scale))
            buf = bytearray()
            _pack_strings(buf, strings)
            _pack_i64(buf, ints[:k_ints])
            _pack_u32(buf, uints[:k_uints])
    return bytes(buf)

import random
import struct
import string
from typing import List

# Target data type: printf-format string and related C-strings/ints used by LogPrint/NEXT_LOG*
# The fuzz stubs pull:
# - level: small unsigned int
# - tag: FUZZ_PARAM_STR() -> C-string
# - format strings: fixed constants inside the stub (so our buffer need not supply them)
# - integers: via FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int)
# - names/strings: via FUZZ_PARAM_STR()
# Therefore, to drive interesting behavior, we should provide a buffer that the fuzzer
# framework will slice into: a sequence of length-prefixed strings mixed with 32-bit
# unsigned ints. Many fuzz frameworks back FUZZ_PARAM_STR and FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int)
# by consuming from a common byte buffer. We'll layout data in a simple, parseable way
# to yield valid C-strings and varied integers.
#
# Buffer layout (little-endian):
# [magic 4B] = b"LOGF"
# [count_u32 4B] = number of entries following
# Then a sequence of entries; each entry is either:
#   - type 1 (u32): [type=1 u8][pad 3B][value u32]
#   - type 2 (string): [type=2 u8][pad 3B][len u16][flags u16][bytes ...][nul 0x00]
# The fuzzer stub will not parse this format explicitly, but typical FUZZ_PARAM readers
# will just read integers/strings in order. By alternating entries, we increase the
# likelihood that reads line up producing valid tags and names. Strings are ASCII/UTF-8
# and null-terminated; include a range of interesting characters.
# We keep total size <= 4096 bytes.

MAX_SIZE = 4096
MAGIC = b"LOGF"

PRINTABLE = string.ascii_letters + string.digits
DELIMS = "-_:/.@#"
SPACES = "  "
PUNCT = "[]{}()"
HEXCHARS = string.hexdigits

def _rand_tag(r: random.Random) -> str:
    # Produce tags typical for logging: components, modules, path-like, with safe chars
    parts = []
    n = r.randint(1, 3)
    for _ in range(n):
        base_len = r.randint(3, 10)
        base = ''.join(r.choice(PRINTABLE) for _ in range(base_len))
        if r.random() < 0.4:
            base += r.choice(DELIMS)
        if r.random() < 0.3:
            base += str(r.randint(0, 999))
        parts.append(base)
    tag = '/'.join(parts) if r.random() < 0.5 else '.'.join(parts)
    if r.random() < 0.2:
        tag = tag.upper()
    return tag[:64]

def _rand_name(r: random.Random) -> str:
    # Strings used for %s argument: include spaces and punctuation but keep safe
    words = []
    m = r.randint(1, 4)
    for _ in range(m):
        wl = r.randint(2, 12)
        word = ''.join(r.choice(PRINTABLE) for _ in range(wl))
        if r.random() < 0.2:
            word += r.choice(PUNCT)
        words.append(word)
    s = r.choice([" ", "-", "_"])
    return s.join(words)[:128]

def _u32(r: random.Random) -> int:
    choice = r.random()
    if choice < 0.12:
        return 0
    if choice < 0.24:
        return 1
    if choice < 0.36:
        return 4
    if choice < 0.48:
        return 5  # useful for %x to show hex digits
    if choice < 0.60:
        return 0xFFFFFFFF
    if choice < 0.72:
        return 0x7FFFFFFF
    if choice < 0.84:
        return 0x80000000
    return r.getrandbits(32)

def _emit_u32(val: int) -> bytes:
    return struct.pack('<I', val & 0xFFFFFFFF)

def _emit_entry_u32(val: int) -> bytes:
    # [type=1][pad][u32]
    return bytes([1, 0, 0, 0]) + _emit_u32(val)

def _emit_entry_str(s: str, r: random.Random) -> bytes:
    b = s.encode('utf-8', 'ignore')
    # Occasionally hex-leaning strings for %x context confusion-resistance
    if r.random() < 0.15 and len(b) < 64:
        hx = ''.join(r.choice(HEXCHARS) for _ in range(r.randint(4, 16)))
        b += b' ' + hx.encode('ascii')
    # Ensure null-terminated
    l = len(b)
    if l > 1000:
        b = b[:1000]
        l = 1000
    # [type=2][pad][len u16][flags u16][data][nul]
    flags = 0
    if r.random() < 0.3:
        flags |= 1  # meaningless to the consumer, but reserved
    return bytes([2, 0, 0, 0]) + struct.pack('<HH', l, flags) + b + b'\x00'

def _build_entries(r: random.Random, budget: int) -> bytes:
    out = bytearray()
    count = 0
    # Start with a tag string to satisfy first FUZZ_PARAM_STR consumers
    first_tag = _rand_tag(r)
    out += _emit_entry_str(first_tag, r)
    count += 1
    # Then a few integers to satisfy levels/values/hex
    for _ in range(r.randint(2, 5)):
        out += _emit_entry_u32(_u32(r))
        count += 1
    # Alternate names and ints
    while len(out) + 16 < budget:
        if r.random() < 0.55:
            out += _emit_entry_str(_rand_name(r), r)
        else:
            out += _emit_entry_u32(_u32(r))
        count += 1
        if count > 200:
            break
    # Prefix with header
    header = bytearray()
    header += MAGIC
    header += _emit_u32(count)
    return bytes(header + out)

def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:
    r = random.Random(seed)
    # Size budget between 256 and 2048 to keep inputs compact yet rich
    budget = r.randint(256, 2048)
    buf = _build_entries(r, min(budget, MAX_SIZE - 8))
    # Ensure overall cap
    return buf[:MAX_SIZE]

import random
from typing import List

def _annexb_start_code() -> bytes:
    # 4-byte Annex B start code
    return b"\x00\x00\x00\x01"

def _gen_h264_header(rnd: random.Random) -> int:
    # Compose an H.264 NAL header byte: F(1)=0, nal_ref_idc(2 bits), nal_unit_type(5 bits)
    forbidden_zero_bit = 0  # must be 0 for valid streams
    nal_ref_idc = rnd.randrange(0, 4)  # 0..3
    # Prefer a spread of interesting types
    interesting_types = [1, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]  # SLICE, IDR, SEI, SPS, PPS, AUD
    if rnd.random() < 0.7:
        nal_unit_type = rnd.choice(interesting_types)
    else:
        nal_unit_type = rnd.randrange(0, 32)
    hdr = (forbidden_zero_bit << 7) | (nal_ref_idc << 5) | (nal_unit_type & 0x1F)
    return hdr & 0xFF

def _gen_hevc_header_bytes(rnd: random.Random) -> bytes:
    # Generate first two bytes of HEVC NAL header after start code.
    # HEVC first header byte bits: forbidden_zero_bit(1)=0, nal_unit_type(6), nuh_layer_id bit5 (MSB of layer id)
    # Second header byte: remaining 5 bits of nuh_layer_id (bits 7..3), and nuh_temporal_id_plus1 (3 bits), must be >=1
    forbidden_zero_bit = 0
    # Prefer interesting non-VCL and IRAP types
    interesting = [32, 33, 34, 35, 19, 20, 21]  # VPS, SPS, PPS, AUD, IDR types, CRA
    if rnd.random() < 0.7:
        nal_unit_type = rnd.choice(interesting)
    else:
        nal_unit_type = rnd.randrange(0, 64)
    # nuh_layer_id is 6 bits total
    nuh_layer_id = rnd.randrange(0, 64)
    # temporal_id_plus1 must be 1..7
    temporal_id_plus1 = rnd.randrange(1, 8)
    byte0 = ((forbidden_zero_bit & 0x1) << 7) | ((nal_unit_type & 0x3F) << 1) | ((nuh_layer_id >> 5) & 0x1)
    byte1 = ((nuh_layer_id & 0x1F) << 3) | (temporal_id_plus1 & 0x7)
    return bytes([byte0 & 0xFF, byte1 & 0xFF])

def _pad_random_payload(rnd: random.Random, min_extra: int, max_total: int) -> bytes:
    # Add some random payload bytes to resemble a fuller NAL unit
    extra_len = rnd.randrange(min_extra, max( min_extra+1, max_total))
    return rnd.randbytes(extra_len)

def _build_buffer(rnd: random.Random) -> bytes:
    # Choose among targeted stub expectations
    mode = rnd.choice(["h264_type", "hevc_type", "h264_ref", "hevc_layer"])

    start = _annexb_start_code()
    # Ensure at least 5 bytes for all but hevc_layer which needs 6
    if mode == "h264_type":
        hdr = _gen_h264_header(rnd)
        buf = bytearray(start + bytes([hdr]))
        # add random payload keeping total <= 4096
        remaining = 4096 - len(buf)
        buf += _pad_random_payload(rnd, 0, remaining)
        return bytes(buf)
    elif mode == "hevc_type":
        # For HEVC type stub, only data[4] used; still make a valid-ish header
        hevc_hdr = _gen_hevc_header_bytes(rnd)
        buf = bytearray(start + bytes([hevc_hdr[0]]))
        remaining = 4096 - len(buf)
        buf += _pad_random_payload(rnd, 0, remaining)
        return bytes(buf)
    elif mode == "h264_ref":
        hdr = _gen_h264_header(rnd)
        buf = bytearray(start + bytes([hdr]))
        remaining = 4096 - len(buf)
        buf += _pad_random_payload(rnd, 0, remaining)
        return bytes(buf)
    else:  # hevc_layer
        hevc_hdr = _gen_hevc_header_bytes(rnd)
        buf = bytearray(start + hevc_hdr)
        remaining = 4096 - len(buf)
        buf += _pad_random_payload(rnd, 0, remaining)
        return bytes(buf)


def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rnd = random.Random(seed)
    return _build_buffer(rnd)
